subject: science
passage: Great frigatebirds can stay aloft over the ocean for weeks at a time, which long raised the question of whether, and how, they sleep. When researchers fitted birds in the Galápagos Islands with small devices that recorded brain activity, they found that the birds did sleep in flight, often letting one half of the brain rest while the other stayed alert. Yet in-flight sleep came in bursts lasting seconds and totaled less than an hour a day, compared with more than twelve hours a day once the birds were back on land. Frigatebirds, it seems, can sleep while flying, but they do remarkably little of it.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Frigatebirds sleep in flight, but far less than they sleep once they are back on land.
choices.B: Frigatebirds rest only one half of the brain at a time whenever they sleep in flight.
choices.C: Frigatebirds need more than twelve hours of sleep a day in order to stay aloft for weeks.
choices.D: Recording devices revealed how long frigatebirds sleep after returning to land.

explanation.why: The text answers its opening question in two parts: the birds "did sleep in flight," "yet" that sleep was brief, under an hour a day versus more than twelve on land. The last sentence states both parts together, so the main idea must include both.
explanation.A: Correct. This keeps both halves of the finding: sleep in flight happens, but it is small compared with sleep on land.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the birds "often" rested half the brain, not that they always did.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Twelve hours is how much the birds slept on land; the text never says they need that much to stay aloft.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is a single detail and misses the main finding about sleep during flight.
